children: Early-stage investors FirstMark Capital and Chemistry Ventures are backing Liquid Compute, a startup looking to set up a regulated exchange for the fast-expanding market for artificial-intelligence computing capacity used by AI developers.

Participants in the $15 million seed investment supporting the New York company include firms such as K8 Capital, Night Capital, TrueBridge and Brainchild Holdings, according to Liquid Compute, which is also backed by Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator.

The breakneck expansion of AI technology is driving demand for access to the graphic processing units that are the main components used to run inference engines and generative or agentic systems. The market for computing capacity, which is measured in hours of GPU use, is expected to reach about $2.3 trillion in value by 2030, a sixfold increase from an estimated $360 billion last year, according to Boston Consulting Group.

But a lack of price transparency and the absence of financial mechanisms such as futures contracts make it difficult for AI developers and suppliers of computing capacity to manage costs, while compute providers have struggled to meet demand, leading to a series of imbalances, the consulting firm and other industry observers say. Liquid Compute envisions a market designed specifically for the suppliers of computing capacity and the AI developers that rely on those systems, which are typically housed in data centers.

The company aims to help develop an exchange akin to electricity markets, whose participants include not only power suppliers and users but also various intermediates that can make bets on prices, said Liquid Compute Chief Executive Ronit Jain. Broader trading is critical to make the AI-computing market more efficient, he said, noting that some data center users lock up large amounts of capacity but then end up not using it for much of their allotted time.

"We believe that compute is a strategic utility similar to electricity, and we believe the absence of financial derivatives has largely caused a massive underutilization of compute as an asset class," Jain said. He co-founded Liquid Compute about two years ago alongside Aarav Patel, who serves as the company's president. Both are 22 years old.

Liquid Compute earlier this year submitted applications to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to establish an exchange to trade AI-computing capacity and a clearinghouse for related financial derivatives such as futures, options and swaps. The applications are pending the regulator's approval.

Capacity suppliers and AI developers face various hurdles, according to industry analysts. For example, the lack of hedging instruments to lock in future computing prices encourages a buy-and-hoard mentality by users, especially large ones, limiting capacity for smaller AI companies that lack the same buying power.

Also, the inability to lock in future revenue through hedge instruments increases risks for providers of computing capacity that sign long-term leases with data-center developers. The elevated uncertainty can make lenders reluctant to provide compute-time suppliers with financing to expand, industry analysts say.

An exchange would help alleviate such problems by facilitating short-term access to idle computing capacity, Jain said. For example, "any AI company that's taken out large compute contracts could resell part of that capacity" on the exchange, he said.

"It will allow not just AI companies and [computing capacity suppliers] to trade, but anyone with a large balance sheet who's interested in speculating on compute as a physical asset," Jain added. He cited hedge funds, brokers and commodity traders as other potential market participants, similar to U.S. power exchanges.

Liquid Compute is also developing price benchmarks based on "standardized technical specifications" of things including processor type used, the location of energy-hungry data centers and their power-grid connections, all of which can affect the underlying cost of computing capacity, Jain said.

The company also plans to introduce purely financial instruments such as futures contracts to help expand the market beyond trading between buyers and sellers of computing capacity. As an example of the role such tools can play, Jain cited a hypothetical data-center operator who signs a one-year computing supply agreement with an AI developer and then buys an option from a financial player to lock in revenue for a longer period, making its business more attractive to lenders.

"Once the physical trading is mature, we will create an ecosystem in which people can trade cash-settled derivatives much more freely as well because there's more liquidity on the physical side," he said.

A number of other companies are also seeking to develop financial instruments around trading AI computing capacity to capitalize on the booming market, from established operators such as Intercontinental Exchange to other startups. The CFTC last month requested public comments on listing financial derivatives that reference the price of access to computing power needed to run the large language models that drive AI inference engines.

Jain said he expects Liquid Compute to benefit from seeking regulatory approval for an AI exchange. He pointed to other startups that have successfully followed a similar approach, such as prediction markets operator Kalshi.
"Becoming CFTC-regulated is certainly the longest and hardest path, but it has shown time and time again that, when an asset commoditizes, regulated players are the ultimate winners," he said.
